speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. In the fall of 1974 the members of the NDP disappeared from the House, leaving one person behind to call the Speaker's attention to the lack of a quorum. Some 42 of us were attending committee meetings, but not one NDP member was in attendance. Today is an NDP opposition day, and look at them. They number four, with one standing behind the curtains drinking coffee.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO COMBAT INFLATION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO COMBAT INFLATION
speechtext: Order, please. That is not a point of order.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO COMBAT INFLATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in July, 1974, the people of Canada had an opportunity to vote in a general election. The main issue which developed during the campaign, an issue on which the people really decided how to vote, was really the suggestion by the Convervative party that inflation in Canada was so serious that what was required to stop the inflationary spiral, so adversely affecting all Canadians, was a 90-day wage and price freeze, following which a Conservative government would work out an incomes policy.
At the time the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) opposed a wage and price freeze, saying it would not work. He said inflation was an international occurrence that could not be stopped or controlled by any one country. The people in Canada by the thousands deserted the Conservative party, and to some extent the NDP, and elected, particularly in Ontario, Liberal member after Liberal member. They voted this way on the basis of the Prime Minister's promise to oppose wage and price controls.
Some 15 months later the Prime Minister, elected on his promise not to impose wage and price controls, comes to the Canadian people and says we must have those controls. He may be right. The situation may have changed, but neither he nor his ministers have yet explained to the satisfaction of the Canadian people what that change has been. Those trained seals who sit behind the Prime Minister, many of whom were elected on the basis of his promise to oppose wage and price controls, expect us to keep quiet and fall in line as they have done. We were not elected as Liberals and we are not obligated to the Prime Minister. We intend to keep asking the same kind of questions we were asking last year.
We have attempted, here in the House and in committee, to find out from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) what the inflationary problem is. We know that in the last year the cost of living has risen by 10.5 per cent. We have asked the Minister of Finance what his experts have told him they expect inflation to be in the next year. We have asked why the government thinks the situation is so serious it has to bring in legislation the like of which we have never seen in Canada in over 100 years, except during wartime. We have asked the Minister of Finance what he expects the anti-inflation program will do, and what the rate of inflation will be after the implementation of this program.
The Minister of Finance has completely rejected all invitations to inform the people about the estimates his experts have made. I think he owes it to the people of Canada to tell them what the situation is. After all, he is
November 14, 1975

proposing controls on all Canadians the like of which we have never seen except during wartime, yet he is refusing to tell us what the situation is, or is expected to be.
Some of us with some contacts have made some inquiries. I have before me the estimates made by a very respected non-partisan and non-political institute, namely, the Institute of Quantitative Analysis of the University of Toronto. Let me place on the record the kind of estimate they made with the help of their computer. Their computer is similar to that used by the Department of Finance.
They estimate that the cost of living for the next year, without the anti-inflation program and the controls the government proposes, would have risen from the IOV2 per cent increase we had in the last year to 11.3 per cent in the coming year. I do not think that is the kind of increase which would necessitate the almost war action the government is proposing.
Let us look at what they tell us the increase in the cost of living will be in the next year with the control program. As a result of this tremendous interference in the lives of the ordinary citizens of Canada, what will the increase in the cost of living be in the next year according to the University of Toronto Institute of Quantitative Analysis? Will it be, instead of IOV2 per cent, 5 per cent, 7 per cent or 8 per cent? In other words, will there be a substantial reduction in the cost of living? According to the Institute of Quantitative Analysis the increase in the coming year will be 9.6 per cent.
After all the mountain of effort we will have a mouselike decrease in the cost of living of less than 1 per cent. But the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Finance say that the people they want to protect, the people who need the assistance, are not the businessmen, the professional people or the organized workers because they can look after themselves. That is what the hon. member for Gloucester said, and he is right. The organized worker will get the 10 per cent which the government says is the maximum he can get. Of course he will get it because he has the economic power. But what about the poor and the unorganized workers whom the hon. member for Gloucester said will be helped by this program?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO COMBAT INFLATION
speechtext: I did not say that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO COMBAT INFLATION
speechtext:
I have in front of me a table prepared by Statistics Canada which shows the percentage of the gross national product each fifth of the population has received for the last 25 years. These figures are very interesting because they answer, I think very well, the simple question asked by the hon. member for Gloucester-what happens to the poor people?
Let us go back 25 years. In 1951 the bottom one-fifth of the people in Canada, the lowest 20 per cent of the workers, received 4.4 per cent of the gross national product.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO COMBAT INFLATION
speechtext: Quite a few of them were in New Brunswick.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO COMBAT INFLATION
speechtext:
Yes, and also in Newfoundland. What did the top 20 per cent receive? They received 42.8 per cent. In
Anti-Inflation Program
1974, 25 years later, again under a Liberal government, the bottom 20 per cent, after all the so-called programs to help the poor people, received .4 per cent less than they received in 1951. What did the top 20 per cent get? They received 42.4 per cent.
I want to place on the record two other very interesting figures. I refer to the figures for 1971 and 1972. That was the last time the Liberal government tried, it said, to do something about inflation and to help the poor people. That is the time John Young and his incomes board were working. What did they accomplish? Here is the record. In 1971 under a Liberal government, with the same Prime Minister, what did the bottom 20 per cent receive in respect of the gross national product? Instead of the 4.4 per cent they received in 1951, they received 3.6 per cent in 1971. What did the top 20 per cent receive 20 years later in 1971? They received 43.3 per cent of the gross national product.
In 1972, while John Young was still charging on his white charger, the bottom 20 per cent received 3.8 per cent of the gross national product while the top 20 per cent received 42.9 per cent of the gross national product. That is an indication of how much the Liberal government and the Liberal Party care about the poor people. Liberal members and the Minister of Finance say-although they originally said that the people at the bottom could get $600 and the people at the top $2,400-in terms of an increase they have looked at it again, have found they made a mistake, and are now giving the people at the bottom $750. How can the people at the bottom get a cent? They are unorganized. How does a woman working as a waitress on Sparks Street get that $750?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO COMBAT INFLATION
speechtext: What would she get without the controls?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO COMBAT INFLATION
speechtext:
I was coming to that. She would get precisely the same wage she is getting now. What we propose, what we proposed the same night the Prime Minister outlined his anti-inflation proposal, and what we have proposed every day since then, and what we are saying to the provincial governments is let the provincial and federal governments get together and bring in legislation to increase the minimum wage. If we are concerned about the people at the bottom that is the way to bring up their income.
I do not say that the minimum wage should be the $4 that I believe has been proposed by the Canadian Labour Congress, but how about a straight 50 cents an hour increase in all jurisdictions, federal and provincial? This is what we should have if we are worried about the poor people. This is a concrete proposal. I will wait for the hon. member for Gloucester to propose that to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). I will make this proposal to the government of Manitoba.
The people at the lowest end of the income scale are not organized. They have no economic power and are at the mercy of their employers. I do not intend to be critical of their employers as individuals because they are engaged in a cut-throat business where, if they increase their wage rate, they are in difficulty unless their competitors do the same. However, an increase in the minimum wage rate would mean that every person at the bottom, including

November 14, 1975
Anti-Inflation Program
every employer, would be treated in the same way. It would not hurt anyone very much. This is what the hon. member for Gloucester was talking about quite eloquently. I hope he meant it seriously. I suggest that this is a quick way to help the people at the bottom.
We are told we are in a crisis situation and must have restraint. We are told that people should not receive an increase of more than 10 per cent, and that if we do this everyone will be treated fairly. I have in front of me a news story which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of October 23, 1975. I wish to read, for the benefit of the hon. member for Gloucester and others, a few sentences from this. It is datelined Ottawa. It reads:
Salary scales of about 1,150 senior public servants were raised between $2,000 and $6,000 a year on Sept. 4 retroactive to last April 1,...
Then further on:
Also affected were about 350 in level 2, the next highest group, 140 in level 3 and about 10 executives in level 4 at the top of the pay scale.
Salaries for senior executives range between a minimum of $27,500 in level 1 and a maximum of $54,000 in level 4.
I think there is something immoral about senior public servants drawing in the neighbourhood of $50,000 per year, sitting down with policy advisers to the Prime Minister and saying that they are in a real serious situation, suggesting limiting the amount anyone's income can be increased in the next year to $2,400, and ignoring the fact that they just received their increase. If the government was serious it should have set an example. If those at the top of the civil service can receive an increase of $5,000 or $6,000 per year, how can we ask others to limit themselves to $2,400?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO COMBAT INFLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO COMBAT INFLATION
speechtext:
It is not my responsibility to fight the battles of any particular group. I am not going to discuss now whether the postal workers are asking for too much or just enough, but I will ask a very simple question: how can we say to the postal worker that he is asking for too much when we have permitted people at the top to receive increases of $5,000 and $6,000 per year?
Let us consider the whole question of restraint. We have said that it is easy to control wages and salaries, and the hon. member for Gloucester is correct when he says that the organized worker will look after himself. If the limit is 10 per cent, the organized worker who receives $10,000 will receive his $1,000. The organized teacher will receive his $2,000, $1,500, or whatever it is. The nurse will receive a large increase.
There is nothing in the white paper, nothing in the speeches made by the minister, and nothing in the discussions held in the finance committee which would give the slightest indication that the government has really worked out a program which will control the incomes of professional people. In answer to questions today the minister said that he is working with the provinces and that he expects they will come to an agreement. We know for a fact that more than one province has said to the minister that this program will not work unless the federal government is prepared to put a 100 per cent surtax on net increases over $2,400 per year.

Of course the provinces will sit down with doctors and work out fee schedules, and of course the provinces can say that they will not increase the rates of fees which are paid, but there is nothing to prevent doctors from seeing more people and doing more work, in which case their income would go up.
If a province were to try to implement a surtax there would be nothing to prevent a doctor from moving from one province which imposed a surtax to another province which did not impose a surtax. That is why some of the provinces have asked the Minister of Finance and his officials to agree to a surtax. I know for a fact that up until now the minister and his officials have simply and completely rejected the idea. That being the case, the claim that the government is being equitable is false. It has no intention of controlling the income of the doctor, the lawyer, the architect, the engineer, and on down the list.
I do not believe this program can work at all. It is the wrong kind of program at the wrong time. Surely one does not have to be overly bright to realize that this program does not have a hope in hell of working if ordinary people do not believe that it is being operated equitably. I say to hon. members opposite that if the ordinary citizen in this country thinks wage and salary controls are for him but not for people in the upper brackets, he simply will not accept them. We will have more strikes than ever before because ordinary people do not believe this is equitable.
It is interesting to note who is doing the striking so far. It is not the long organized blue collar workers. They have not been on strike. Possibly a few of them have been on strike since this program was inaugurated, but who is on strike? Teachers, nurses, and the kind of people who, until a few years ago, would have recoiled in horror if anyone had suggested for a moment that they were part of the labour movement or the working class, are those who are now on strike.
I do not have much time left, but I wish to say that what I have said about professional people is just as true for corporations. A senior official in Revenue Canada at a meeting a week or so ago spelled out in detail how corporations, and particularly multi-national corporations, can juggle the books, how they can allocate supposed costs to different aspects of business, how they can move hundreds of millions of dollars and how they have the staff to do it, and Revenue Canada does not have the staff to control it. These companies will increase their income and their profits. The ordinary person will be restricted, and those at the bottom will do even worse in the next year than they have done in the last year. For all those reasons it is our intention to oppose this legislation and to support this motion.
